claims.text: The equiatomic Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy contains approximately 25 at.% each Fe, Ni, Cr, and Mn.
The Co-free alloy is a conventionally cast, single-phase solid solution without secondary phases or precipitates.
Removing Co from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi shifts the stacking-fault energy.
Temperature and strain rate jointly control a transition between dislocation glide and mechanical twinning in Co-free FeNiCrMn.
The transition between dislocation glide and mechanical twinning accounts for the alloy's strength–ductility balance under different dynamic conditions.
Temperature- and strain-rate-dependent variations in effective stacking-fault energy control whether dislocation slip or mechanical twinning is activated.
Lower temperatures and/or higher strain rates reduce the effective stacking-fault energy.
Reduced effective stacking-fault energy promotes mechanical twinning.
Mechanical twinning enhances ductility without severely compromising strength.
Higher temperatures and lower strain rates increase the effective stacking-fault energy and favor dislocation glide.
The dislocation-glide-dominated regime has lower yield strength.
At lower temperatures and higher strain rates, Co-free FeNiCrMn will have greater twin density than equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
At lower temperatures and higher strain rates, Co-free FeNiCrMn will exhibit both higher strength and higher ductility than equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
At higher temperatures, dislocation slip will dominate in Co-free FeNiCrMn and its strength will be lower than that of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
The Co-containing equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi baseline has a different stacking-fault energy and dislocation-activity regime from Co-free FeNiCrMn.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloy remains a single-phase solid solution, nominally over approximately 77–773 K.
Outside the stated phase-stability and temperature boundaries, phase transformations or precipitation may change the deformation mechanisms.
The quantitative effect of Co removal on stacking-fault energy and its temperature dependence is not fully characterized.
